changed_pages.previous_text: 55 4 Asset management 4.1 Maintenance and repairs Maintenance keeps UgIFT assets working for the services they were bought to support. Most of the verified assets are furniture, clinical equipment and computers in daily use at Health Centres and seed schools, where wear and breakage are to be expected. Routine checks, a record of faults and a dependable route for repair decide whether a broken item returns to use quickly or stays out of service. During the verification, each facility was asked how it maintains, repairs, services or replaces UgIFT assets and whether it keeps a regular record of their functionality or breakdown. Repair arrangements. Of the 469 facilities that described their maintenance arrangements, 260 (55.4%) met repairs at facility level, from their own funds or with their own staff. Health Centres named Primary Health Care funds (94 of 278, 33.8%), while schools named the capitation or Universal Secondary Education grant, parents' contributions or the school budget (52 of 191, 27.2%). Busaale Health Centre III in Kayunga used Primary Health Care funds for repairs, and Kagumba Seed Secondary School in Kamuli had repaired broken furniture during the second term. A facility could describe more than one arrangement. Support from outside the facility was cited by 152 facilities (32.4%): district offices, mainly the District Health Officer, 85 (18.1%); regional referral hospital workshops or national teams 52 (11.1%); hired technicians and artisans 27 (5.8%); and contra ctors or suppliers under defects liability, guarantee or warranty 12 (2.6%). Major medical equipment repairs depended on this support. Todora Health Centre III in Nwoya worked through the District Health Officer and the Gulu Regional Referral Hospital technical team, Avogera Health Centre III in Buliisa received support from Hoima Regional Referral Hospital, and Bundimulangya Health Centre III in Bundibugyo obtained a team through the District Health Officer. In all, 97 facilities (20.7%), 59 of them schools, had not yet needed maintenance because the assets were new, not yet handed over or the buildings were still under construction, and 36 (7.7%) reported no repair arrangement, with broken items set aside or not repaired. Funds for maintenance and repair were reported as insufficient, particularly for major repairs, by 32 of the 505 facilities that described maintenance or challenges (6.3%). At Kyankaramata Health Centre III in Kyenjojo, Primary Health Care funds met minor repairs, but the cost of major repairs was a constraint. Figure 46 compares these arrangements at Health Centres and seed schools. Health Centres relied more on outside technical support (41.4% of health centres against 19.4% of schools), while schools more often had not yet needed maintenance (30.9% against 13.7%).
